raw_comment:
What do you notice?
- Productivity is the only thing that is increasing.  We are stagnant in level of education and dropping in every other measure.  

What do you wonder?
- I wonder how much of our response to COVID impacted our social and economic issues. 

- I wonder what we are doing wrong in our education that we have not seen a change in our level but we have seen a change in our GDP, life expectancy, etc.  

- I wonder are we focusing on the wrong issues. 

How does this relate to you and your community?

This relates to me and my community because our generation will be called upon to fix this.  We need to figure out what steps need to be focused on so we can grow as a nation and progress together in society!  Obviously something is not working right now, and the problems need to be addressed! 


My Title for the graphs would be:  Where are we going wrong?

raw_comment:
I notice that despite the steadiness or increasing rates of GDP and Productivity, the overall Life Satisfaction within the US has been slowly decreasing and continues to do so, However, other countries that might not have as much productivity have much higher rates of Life Satisfaction. I wonder why they chose orange for these graph lines when purple would have been much better in my professional opinion. As we grow up in this world, especially the US, we have been given the expectation to work as hard as we can and be as productive as possible only for our Life Satisfaction not to reflect the effort we're expected to put into our country.

Title: Working Hard or Hardly Working: Is Corporate America Worth it?

A set of **slope charts / rank-change line charts** showing country rankings between two years for several metrics.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: the visualization is split into multiple panels, one per metric:
  - Total G.D.P.
  - Productivity
  - Life satisfaction
  - Life expectancy
  - Trust in the federal government
  - Social isolation
  - Average years of education
- Within each panel, many country rank trajectories are shown as lines between two time points.
- **Highlighting**: the U.S. is emphasized with a thicker orange line; other countries are shown in thin gray lines.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Metric / indicator (Total G.D.P., Productivity, Life satisfaction, Life expectancy, Trust in the federal government, Social isolation, Average years of education) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Year | Temporal | Horizontal position as the two endpoints in each panel; year labels at top |
| Rank | Ordinal | Vertical position on y-axis; numeric rank labels |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual line identity across the two years |
| Highlight status (U.S. vs. other countries) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue and line weight (orange thick line for U.S., gray thin lines for others) |
| U.S. label / country annotation | Categorical/nominal | Text label (“U.S.” / “United States”) placed near highlighted line |
| Rank value annotations for highlighted country | Ordinal | Numeric text labels at line endpoints |

## 1) Chart type
A set of **slope charts / rank-change line charts** showing country rankings between two years for several metrics.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: the visualization is split into multiple panels, one per metric:
  - Total G.D.P.
  - Productivity
  - Life satisfaction
  - Life expectancy
  - Trust in the federal government
  - Social isolation
  - Average years of education
- Within each panel, many country rank trajectories are shown as lines between two time points.
- **Highlighting**: the U.S. is emphasized with a thicker orange line; other countries are shown in thin gray lines.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|

| Year | Temporal | Horizontal position as the two endpoints in each panel; year labels at top |
| Rank | Ordinal | Vertical position on y-axis; numeric rank labels |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual line identity across the two years |
| Highlight status (U.S. vs. other countries) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue and line weight (orange thick line for U.S., gray thin lines for others) |
| U.S. label / country annotation | Categorical/nominal | Text label (“U.S.” / “United States”) placed near highlighted line |
| Rank value annotations for highlighted country | Ordinal | Numeric text labels at line endpoints |
raw_comment:
We notice that life satisfaction and total GDP has gone down. We notice that we are still higher ranked in total GDP than productivity and life satisfaction.

We wonder where our productivity is going since our GDP and satisfaction is going down? Then why are we being productive?

This affects us and our community because it can compare us to the rest of the world to see how different our lives are compared to other places. 

"From Dollars to Joy: The Evolution of America's Economic and Emotional Landscape"

|---|---|---|

raw_comment: One of the pictures depicts three graphs that show how the United States ranks compared to other countries in total GDP, productivity, and life satisfaction (2006-2023). The other picture depicts four graphs that show how the U.S. ranks compared to other income-level countries and China in terms of life expectancy, trust in the government, social isolation, and average years of education. One thing I noticed is that the U.S dropped from 5th to 10th in life satisfaction from 2006-2023. I also noticed that the trust in the government plummeted the most from 20th to 34th in trust in the government. The United States's average years of education is the only rank they have stayed the same in. I wonder why life expectancy in the U.S. has dropped so much. Could it be because of pollution and chemicals in our food? I also wonder why, even though productivity has increased and we are 2nd in total GDP, our life satisfaction is so much lower. This relates to me and my community because I live in the U.S., and although we are ranked high in economy and education, our country seems to be dealing with a lot of dissatisfaction, distrust in our government, and social isolation. This makes me think about how the U.S. government has so much pride in itself, but the citizens are struggling.

raw_comment:
Is America Really Still the Land of Opportunity: New Data Shows Quality of Life in the U.S. on the Decline

What do you notice?
I noticed that all of the graphs except for productivity and average years of education decreased over time. 

What do you wonder?

I wonder how the scholars went about collecting the data, and if they used surveys or some other type of method to collect it. I also wonder if they even had participants, and if so, how did they select them?

How does this relate to you and your community?

I think that a lot may be connected to social media and the increased use of technology. Things like life satisfaction and social isolation can be directly tied to the effects of social media, since they create impossible ideals that people try to live up to and can't. Productivity probably increased because technology has made things more efficient, allowing us to complete things faster. As far as the lowered life expectancy, that could be related to increased poverty, stress, vaping, and many other interrelated issues. Trust in the federal government has decreased due to an exponential jump in the instability of both domestic and international issues.

raw_comment:
Headline: America: Money over happiness?
After reading and analyzing the various graphs, I noticed that in the United States, there has been both an increase and a decrease in certain aspects. I see a slight increase in productivity and a small decrease in life satisfaction. I also notice a significant decline in trust in the government, social isolation, and life expectancy. I also saw a ranking for each country in each graph. For example, in social isolation, the U.S. was ranked number 2 in 2006; in 2022, they are ranked lower at 10.I wonder what contributes to the fall/increase in the ratings and the change in the amount of aspects of G.P.D, productivity, life satisfaction, etc. I think the graph encourages readers to brainstorm why this may be happening. As well as surmise any correlations between the two. In my opinion, I think that an increment in productivity and a decrease in life satisfaction could be related. This graph relates to my community and me because I live in the U.S., and it is essential to be aware of the state of my country. This graph reveals many problems that affect me, my community, and many other people around the country. For example, the significant decline in trust in the government is an issue for the people. The lack of trust in world leaders contributes to today's many political problems. This graph reveals that strengthening aspects like trust in government is a significant concern that benefits our country.

raw_comment:
I've noticed that while America's GDP and life expectancy have declined, productivity has increased. This could indicate that although the nation is highly productive, the social framework and its citizens' mental well-being and health may suffer. 

I wonder why the U.S. has dramatically declined trust in the government and life satisfaction. Is increased productivity coming at the expense of individual well-being?

This relates to my community because it is essential to recognize that life satisfaction is declining. Even though productivity in the U.S. is increasing, it doesn't change the reality that people aren't satisfied with their lives. 

Title: The Polarization of the United States! Prosperity doesn't guarantee quality of life

If these trends continue, my community and I will have to take into consideration how they will affect our future life plans, such as retirement plans. Headline: "Is the United States Choosing the Economy Over its People?"

raw_comment:
I notice the GDP ranking of America going from #1 to #2.  I also noticed a decrease in life satisfaction, life expectancy, and a decrease in trust in the federal government.  As well as an increase in social isolation and productivity compared to other high-income countries.


I wonder why the same timeframe wasn’t used for all graphs.  I also wonder what exactly has caused all these negative effects in the USA.  


The graphs relate to me and my community because they directly relate and reflect changes seen all over the world and in the USA, hence me and my community.  The social and economic changes have also been noticed in my personal life and in the life of many people.


“America: The Next Fallen Rome”

raw_comment:
Seven different graphs portray the rankings of the United States compared to other developed countries in several different categories. It also looks at where we were ranked around twenty years ago compared to now. For example, the US is currently ranked second in total GDP. However, in 1990, it was ranked first. I wonder which country replaced the US as the highest in total GDP. Life expectancy, life satisfaction, and trust in the federal government scores have all gone down which could potentially be very concerning for the United States. The only ranking that stayed consistent was the average years of education. I wonder what made our ranking in social isolation improve, since it has seemed like that problem has only gotten worse. This impacts my community because I live in the United States and the fact that most of these rankings have become more negative means that there are issues harming the American people that need to be addressed.
Headline: Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness

1. After looking at the graph, I noticed that it compares the overall success of people in the United States to other countries. 4. A headline for this graph is "Prosperity in the United States Compared to Other Countries."

raw_comment:
Thanks to all the students who responded.   Here are some of the catchy headlines we received:  “We Aren't Happy and We're Dying Young ... But at Least We're Working Hard!” by Sienna and Olivia of Tenakill Middle School in Closter, N.J., "Shifting Prosperity: U.S. Faces Declining Satisfaction Amidst Economic Gains" by Lily at Academy of Saint Elizabeth, Convent Station, N.J. and three headlines from Perth Amboy High School, N.J. –“Money Buys Happiness? U.S. Prosperity and Global Quality of Life” by Lavon, “Big Bucks, Small Smiles: What's Going On, USA?” by Johan and "Rich in GDP, Poor in Spirit: America’s Happiness in Deficit?" by Daniel.

Please return on Friday when we will reveal the free link to the article, a summary of the article, additional questions, shout outs for some of the best headlines for the graph and Stat Nuggets -- definitions of words that relate to the graph and where you can find them in the graph.

The next graph will be released by Friday, April 11.  The topic is how we’ve changed since Covid.

Signing off – Sharon Hessney from Boston who is mindful about the wealth gap that causes, in part, the unhappiness, and Kristina Barnaby of Fairfield, Conn., who fights social isolation by taking long walks with her family and dog.

raw_comment:
Headline- Trouble in Paradise

What I notice:
Seven different graphs highlight the United States specifically in categories that measure prosperity and quality of life. I noticed that in total GDP, the U.S. held the #1 spot in 1990, but by 2023 it had slipped to #2. Surprisingly, the U.S. only ranks 10th in productivity. Despite being such a wealthy country, the U.S. has seen a drop in both life satisfaction and life expectancy, which is quite concerning. Trust in the federal government has also plummeted, as well as social isolation. The only steady metric is the average years of education. 

What I wonder:
Why did the U.S. drop so much in life satisfaction, life expectancy, and trust in the federal government, all in a matter of a couple of years? Could this be a product of the extreme political polarization or the economy? Also, what’s holding back productivity in such a wealthy nation? Why is social isolation also still so low? Did COVID affect these results a lot?

How does this relate to me and my community?
This relates to me and my community because I live in the U.S., and I see people working hard every day, like my parents, but they are still stressed. People I know deal with so many health issues or feel unhappy; that doesn't seem to happen in other countries. Now, more than ever, many don’t trust the government and are extremely skeptical. Although our economy may seem fine, people are generally unhappy in the country.

raw_comment:
Headline: "America: Rich in Economy, Poor in Happiness"

One of the pictures depicts three graphs that show how the United States ranks compared to other countries in total GDP, productivity, and life satisfaction (2006-2023). The other picture depicts four graphs that show how the U.S. ranks compared to other income-level countries and China in terms of life expectancy, trust in the government, social isolation, and average years of education. One thing I noticed is that the U.S dropped from 5th to 10th in life satisfaction from 2006-2023. I also noticed that the trust in the government plummeted the most from 20th to 34th in trust in the government. The United States's average years of education is the only rank they have stayed the same in. I wonder why life expectancy in the U.S. has dropped so much. Could it be because of pollution and chemicals in our food? I also wonder why, even though productivity has increased and we are 2nd in total GDP, our life satisfaction is so much lower. This relates to me and my community because I live in the U.S., and although we are ranked high in economy and education, our country seems to be dealing with a lot of dissatisfaction, distrust in our government, and social isolation. This makes me think about how the U.S. government has so much pride in itself, but the citizens are struggling.

raw_comment:
The graph shows the prosperity and quality of life of the United States compared to 38 other countries, and that the United States was ranked number one for Total G.D.P. in 1990, but dropped to number two by 2023.  I also noticed that in terms of the high-income countries that were ranked, the U.S. moved up from 13th to 10th in the Productivity ranking, but moved down from 5th to 10th in the Life satisfaction ranking.  The United States seemed to have dropped from 1 to 2 overall in 2020, so COVID-19 may have had an impact on their ranking.  I wonder why the United States dropped so low on the Life expectancy, Social isolation, and Trust in the federal government ranking.  This also may have had something to do with the lasting effects of COVID-19.  I also wonder why the Average years of education ranking is the only ranking that remained the same from the years it recorded.  This relates to me and my community because I am a citizen of the United States, and this information can affect my community and my future.

raw_comment: In these graphs, I first noticed that the US has dropped in areas of Total GDP, life satisfaction, life expectancy, trust in the government, and social isolation. However, the US has risen in areas of productivity and stayed stable in the amount of time spent in education. I also wonder how the recent tariffs placed by President Trump will impact our total GDP since we import a lot of our goods from foreign countries. raw_comment: This graph shows that the United States was ranked first for G.D.P.  in 1990, but in 2023 it was ranked second. raw_comment:
This graph shows America's shift in success in different areas. In 1990, the United States ranked first in G.D.P, but dropped to second by 2023. This is likely due to to Covid 19, as consumer spending was down during this time. I noticed the country that is first in G.D.P  was ranked 7th in 1990, a very impressive increase.The US increased in productivity going from 13th in 2005 to 10th in 2023. However, the US dropped in life satisfaction, going from 5th to 10th over the course of 16 years. This reflects how living in America has become increasingly hard due to inflation, and high taxes, and other negative economic factors.
2. I wonder what countries are currently first in these categories. I wonder what countries rank the lowest. I wonder what factors have caused worse GDP and life satisfaction in the US. What can the gov. do to improve these statistics?
3. This relates to me because I am a US citizen and these factors affect my life and future. 
4.  America's Fall from Grace

raw_comment:
The prosperity and quality of life in the United States, as measured by seven key indicators, reveals several shifts over time. I notice from 1990 to 2023, the country's total GDP rank dropped from 1st to 2nd, while other countries experienced varying degrees of rise and fall. Additionally, productivity in the U.S. improved, rising from 13th to 10th between 2005 and 2023. However, life satisfaction decreased from 5th to 10th place between 2006 and 2022, and social isolation significantly worsened, dropping from 2nd to 10th in the same period. Along with this, life expectancy declined, and there was a decrease in trust in the federal government. The changes in U.S. performance on these indicators may reflect broader trends affecting my community, such as shifts in economic growth, social dynamics, and trust in government. I wonder how these national shifts are impacting us locally—are we seeing declines in life satisfaction, more isolation, or less trust in leaders? What can local governments do to address these issues and rebuild trust? The decline in social connections signals challenges for communities trying to stay united. Despite the U.S. being an economic powerhouse, these trends may threaten our overall well-being and security.
Headline: "Shifting Prosperity: U.S. Faces Declining Satisfaction Amidst Economic Gains".

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
A set of **slope charts / rank-change line charts** showing country rankings between two years for several metrics.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: the visualization is split into multiple panels, one per metric:
  - Total G.D.P.
  - Productivity
  - Life satisfaction
  - Life expectancy
  - Trust in the federal government
  - Social isolation
  - Average years of education
- Within each panel, many country rank trajectories are shown as lines between two time points.
- **Highlighting**: the U.S. is emphasized with a thicker orange line; other countries are shown in thin gray lines.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Metric / indicator (Total G.D.P., Productivity, Life satisfaction, Life expectancy, Trust in the federal government, Social isolation, Average years of education) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Year | Temporal | Horizontal position as the two endpoints in each panel; year labels at top |
| Rank | Ordinal | Vertical position on y-axis; numeric rank labels |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual line identity across the two years |
| Highlight status (U.S. vs. other countries) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue and line weight (orange thick line for U.S., gray thin lines for others) |
| U.S. label / country annotation | Categorical/nominal | Text label (“U.S.” / “United States”) placed near highlighted line |
| Rank value annotations for highlighted country | Ordinal | Numeric text labels at line endpoints |

I also wonder why the G.D.P. has dropped since 1990, and what countries are being compared to the United States. This graph relates to my community because I live in the United States and it concerns me that the life satisfaction has decreased so much in the past years.

raw_comment:
This graph shows a decrease in Gross Domestic Product and life satisfaction but an increase in productivity. This insinuates that being financially successful and happy in America has become harder. I also noticed that this graph compares 37 high-income countries and China. I found this interesting because while China has a high GDP and rate of productivity, it is not a high-income country. Another thing I noticed was that the education ranking in America stayed the same. I wonder what factors contributed to changing America's rankings in these categories. Most rankings have decreased, so many factors in America in the past 30 years must have made quality of life poorer. I also wonder how other countries fit into this ranking. This relates to my community because, as an American, the quality of life for Americans directly impacts me. If the prosperity of the United States is declining, then the likelihood of prosperity for myself and others is also declining. 
Headline: The decline of prosperity in America.

I also notice that the graphs are showing the United States apart from other countries, and just focusing on it rather than other countries. This relates to me and my community because the economy, social isolation, and all the other graphs are very important to keep in mind and understand because this data reflects us as citizens. We should understand what we need to do better in society or what we need to maintain.

## 1) Chart type
A set of **slope charts / rank-change line charts** showing country rankings between two years for several metrics.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: the visualization is split into multiple panels, one per metric:
  - Total G.D.P.
  - Productivity
  - Life satisfaction
  - Life expectancy
  - Trust in the federal government
  - Social isolation
  - Average years of education
- Within each panel, many country rank trajectories are shown as lines between two time points.
- **Highlighting**: the U.S. is emphasized with a thicker orange line; other countries are shown in thin gray lines.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Metric / indicator (Total G.D.P., Productivity, Life satisfaction, Life expectancy, Trust in the federal government, Social isolation, Average years of education) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Year | Temporal | Horizontal position as the two endpoints in each panel; year labels at top |
| Rank | Ordinal | Vertical position on y-axis; numeric rank labels |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual line identity across the two years |
| Highlight status (U.S. vs. other countries) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue and line weight (orange thick line for U.S., gray thin lines for others) |
| U.S. label / country annotation | Categorical/nominal | Text label (“U.S.” / “United States”) placed near highlighted line |
| Rank value annotations for highlighted country | Ordinal | Numeric text labels at line endpoints |

A set of **slope charts / rank-change line charts** showing country rankings between two years for several metrics.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: the visualization is split into multiple panels, one per metric:
  - Total G.D.P.
  - Productivity
  - Life satisfaction
  - Life expectancy
  - Trust in the federal government
  - Social isolation
  - Average years of education
- Within each panel, many country rank trajectories are shown as lines between two time points.
- **Highlighting**: the U.S. is emphasized with a thicker orange line; other countries are shown in thin gray lines.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Metric / indicator (Total G.D.P., Productivity, Life satisfaction, Life expectancy, Trust in the federal government, Social isolation, Average years of education) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Year | Temporal | Horizontal position as the two endpoints in each panel; year labels at top |
| Rank | Ordinal | Vertical position on y-axis; numeric rank labels |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual line identity across the two years |
| Highlight status (U.S. vs. other countries) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue and line weight (orange thick line for U.S., gray thin lines for others) |
| U.S. label / country annotation | Categorical/nominal | Text label (“U.S.” / “United States”) placed near highlighted line |
| Rank value annotations for highlighted country | Ordinal | Numeric text labels at line endpoints |

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
A set of **slope charts / rank-change line charts** showing country rankings between two years for several metrics.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: the visualization is split into multiple panels, one per metric:
  - Total G.D.P.
  - Productivity
  - Life satisfaction
  - Life expectancy
  - Trust in the federal government
  - Social isolation
  - Average years of education
- Within each panel, many country rank trajectories are shown as lines between two time points.
- **Highlighting**: the U.S. is emphasized with a thicker orange line; other countries are shown in thin gray lines.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Metric / indicator (Total G.D.P., Productivity, Life satisfaction, Life expectancy, Trust in the federal government, Social isolation, Average years of education) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Year | Temporal | Horizontal position as the two endpoints in each panel; year labels at top |
| Rank | Ordinal | Vertical position on y-axis; numeric rank labels |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual line identity across the two years |
| Highlight status (U.S. vs. other countries) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue and line weight (orange thick line for U.S., gray thin lines for others) |
| U.S. label / country annotation | Categorical/nominal | Text label (“U.S.” / “United States”) placed near highlighted line |
| Rank value annotations for highlighted country | Ordinal | Numeric text labels at line endpoints |
raw_comment: This graph compares the United States in many categories to other countries. I noticed that life satisfaction, life expectancy, and social isolation all got worse. I correlate these together because they all include people’s happiness or how people are affected. These could have gotten worse with the Covid pandemic in 2020. I also noticed that productivity went up while life satisfaction went down. I assume this is a result of the use of automation and AI for jobs that replaced humans; this decreases jobs so many people cannot get work, hence why they are unsatisfied. I wonder why GDP went down when productivity went up. Could this be because jobs are being outsourced to low-cost countries? I also wonder if this will change with what the new administration is putting in place. The average years of education relate to myself and my community because it shows education is still prioritized in the US. A title could be: “The United States: for better or worse?”

raw_comment:
Observations - The US maintains a high GDP ranking. Its productivity metric has been steadily rising since 2005, but its social and wellbeing metrics, like life satisfaction and trust in the government, are all declining. It shows how economic strength doesn’t necessarily equate to the overall health of a society. 

Questions - Is increased productivity coming at the expense of individual wellbeing? Is there a correlation between economic growth and the decline in social satisfaction? Additionally, how much does the political climate affect the trust in the federal government?

Relation to Community - Living in NJ, these trends are concerning. It is imperative to think about the pressures we face in our daily lives and whether our focus on economic success is overshadowing our quality of life. People are struggling with the feeling of disconnection and a lack of faith in our institutions.

raw_comment:
1)These charts show how the U.S. ranks among high-income countries over time in several key areas. While the U.S. maintains its top rank in total GDP from 1990 to 2023, it falls behind in several quality-of-life indicators. Life expectancy drops from 19th to 29th, and trust in the federal government plunges from 20th to 34th. The U.S. also becomes more socially isolated, slipping from 2nd to 10th, while its average years of education ranking remains steady at 4th. Despite high productivity and wealth, the decline in well-being metrics suggests broader societal challenges.
2)I also wonder how these rankings would look if broken down by region within the U.S., since national averages might mask significant internal differences in health, education, and social well-being
3)Living in New Jersey, I definitely see some of these trends play out around me. There's a lot of talk and frustration about the government, and it feels like trust in federal leadership has really dropped over the years. A set of **slope charts / rank-change line charts** showing country rankings between two years for several metrics.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: the visualization is split into multiple panels, one per metric:
  - Total G.D.P.
  - Productivity
  - Life satisfaction
  - Life expectancy
  - Trust in the federal government
  - Social isolation
  - Average years of education
- Within each panel, many country rank trajectories are shown as lines between two time points.
- **Highlighting**: the U.S. is emphasized with a thicker orange line; other countries are shown in thin gray lines.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Metric / indicator (Total G.D.P., Productivity, Life satisfaction, Life expectancy, Trust in the federal government, Social isolation, Average years of education) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Year | Temporal | Horizontal position as the two endpoints in each panel; year labels at top |
| Rank | Ordinal | Vertical position on y-axis; numeric rank labels |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual line identity across the two years |
| Highlight status (U.S. vs. other countries) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue and line weight (orange thick line for U.S., gray thin lines for others) |
| U.S. label / country annotation | Categorical/nominal | Text label (“U.S.” / “United States”) placed near highlighted line |
| Rank value annotations for highlighted country | Ordinal | Numeric text labels at line endpoints |

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that the U.S. used to be the 1st in total G.D.P out of other countries since the 90s, but in recent years has been trumped by another country. I also noticed that the U.S. is almost the lowest country in the category of trust in the federal government. There's been many decreases for the U.S., such as, life satisfaction, life expectancy, and more. I also notice nearly all of the graphs are starting from different years.
2. I wonder how the trust in the U.S. government has gone down so fast every single year since 2006. Why has life satisfaction and life expectancy gone down so much in the U.S.? Why are all of the graphs starting from different years?
3. This relates to my community and I because we all live in the country described in each graph, the United States. Although things don't seem too horrible, things seem to be getting worse and worse around here, as shown in a few of the graphs. Sometimes it feels like things are only worsening here in the U.S., rather than getting better, and many citizens in my area can agree to this. 

HEADLINE: Where's the American Dream?: The United States has Lost Itself and We're Getting Replaced

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
A set of **slope charts / rank-change line charts** showing country rankings between two years for several metrics.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: the visualization is split into multiple panels, one per metric:
  - Total G.D.P.
  - Productivity
  - Life satisfaction
  - Life expectancy
  - Trust in the federal government
  - Social isolation
  - Average years of education
- Within each panel, many country rank trajectories are shown as lines between two time points.
- **Highlighting**: the U.S. is emphasized with a thicker orange line; other countries are shown in thin gray lines.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Metric / indicator (Total G.D.P., Productivity, Life satisfaction, Life expectancy, Trust in the federal government, Social isolation, Average years of education) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Year | Temporal | Horizontal position as the two endpoints in each panel; year labels at top |
| Rank | Ordinal | Vertical position on y-axis; numeric rank labels |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual line identity across the two years |
| Highlight status (U.S. vs. other countries) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue and line weight (orange thick line for U.S., gray thin lines for others) |
| U.S. label / country annotation | Categorical/nominal | Text label (“U.S.” / “United States”) placed near highlighted line |
| Rank value annotations for highlighted country | Ordinal | Numeric text labels at line endpoints |

|---|---|---|

| Rank | Ordinal | Vertical position on y-axis; numeric rank labels |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual line identity across the two years |

## 1) Chart type
A set of **slope charts / rank-change line charts** showing country rankings between two years for several metrics.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: the visualization is split into multiple panels, one per metric:
  - Total G.D.P.
  - Productivity
  - Life satisfaction
  - Life expectancy
  - Trust in the federal government
  - Social isolation
  - Average years of education
- Within each panel, many country rank trajectories are shown as lines between two time points.
- **Highlighting**: the U.S. is emphasized with a thicker orange line; other countries are shown in thin gray lines.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Metric / indicator (Total G.D.P., Productivity, Life satisfaction, Life expectancy, Trust in the federal government, Social isolation, Average years of education) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Year | Temporal | Horizontal position as the two endpoints in each panel; year labels at top |
| Rank | Ordinal | Vertical position on y-axis; numeric rank labels |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual line identity across the two years |
| Highlight status (U.S. vs. other countries) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue and line weight (orange thick line for U.S., gray thin lines for others) |
| U.S. label / country annotation | Categorical/nominal | Text label (“U.S.” / “United States”) placed near highlighted line |
| Rank value annotations for highlighted country | Ordinal | Numeric text labels at line endpoints |

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
I notice that the United States went from being ranked number 1 to number 2 in the total G.D.P. I also noticed that many countries had jumped around the ranks for total GDP, specifically towards the bottom of the ranks. The country ranked number 7 had a very big jump, it had gone from being ranked number 7 to being ranked number 1 between the years of 1990 to 2023. I noticed that for productivity, the U.S. had gone from 13 to 10 between the years of 2005 to 2023. The life satisfaction for the United States had dropped from being ranked number 5 to being ranked number 10 between the years of 2006 to 2022. 

2. What do you wonder?
Why has the U.S. gone from being ranked number 1 to number 2 in the last 33  years? What country was ranked number 7 in 1990, and what did they do to become the number 1 ranked country for Gross National Product? What led the United States to become number 10 in life satisfaction? 

3. How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because some of these things are already slowly showing in my community, especially since the increase in tariffs. 

4. Catchy Headline
“Unpacking the Data: What Seven Key Metrics Reveal About U.S. Prosperity and Global Quality of Life”

A set of **slope charts / rank-change line charts** showing country rankings between two years for several metrics.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: the visualization is split into multiple panels, one per metric:
  - Total G.D.P.
  - Productivity
  - Life satisfaction
  - Life expectancy
  - Trust in the federal government
  - Social isolation
  - Average years of education
- Within each panel, many country rank trajectories are shown as lines between two time points.
- **Highlighting**: the U.S. is emphasized with a thicker orange line; other countries are shown in thin gray lines.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Metric / indicator (Total G.D.P., Productivity, Life satisfaction, Life expectancy, Trust in the federal government, Social isolation, Average years of education) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Year | Temporal | Horizontal position as the two endpoints in each panel; year labels at top |
| Rank | Ordinal | Vertical position on y-axis; numeric rank labels |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual line identity across the two years |
| Highlight status (U.S. vs. other countries) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue and line weight (orange thick line for U.S., gray thin lines for others) |
| U.S. label / country annotation | Categorical/nominal | Text label (“U.S.” / “United States”) placed near highlighted line |
| Rank value annotations for highlighted country | Ordinal | Numeric text labels at line endpoints |

This is just a scenario, it's not relevant to all people, but based on the graphs, it probably is.

## 1) Chart type
A set of **slope charts / rank-change line charts** showing country rankings between two years for several metrics.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: the visualization is split into multiple panels, one per metric:
  - Total G.D.P.
  - Productivity
  - Life satisfaction
  - Life expectancy
  - Trust in the federal government
  - Social isolation
  - Average years of education
- Within each panel, many country rank trajectories are shown as lines between two time points.
- **Highlighting**: the U.S. is emphasized with a thicker orange line; other countries are shown in thin gray lines.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Metric / indicator (Total G.D.P., Productivity, Life satisfaction, Life expectancy, Trust in the federal government, Social isolation, Average years of education) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Year | Temporal | Horizontal position as the two endpoints in each panel; year labels at top |
| Rank | Ordinal | Vertical position on y-axis; numeric rank labels |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual line identity across the two years |
| Highlight status (U.S. vs. other countries) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue and line weight (orange thick line for U.S., gray thin lines for others) |
| U.S. label / country annotation | Categorical/nominal | Text label (“U.S.” / “United States”) placed near highlighted line |
| Rank value annotations for highlighted country | Ordinal | Numeric text labels at line endpoints |

raw_comment:
I notice that both the U.S ranking of life expectancy and social isolation have both dropped over years. In 1990 U.S was ranked #19 in life expectancy and then dropped to #29 in 2023. In 2006 U.S was ranked #2 in social isolation, but went down to #10 by 2022. 

I wonder if the social isolation of the U.S has an effect on life expectancy? When the social isolation of the U.S decreases, does that cause the life expectancy to decrease too?

This relates to our community because when people feel isolated it can lead to stress, mental health struggles, and more. This can have a big effect on our community and how people live. 

How Social isolation Affects Lives

  - Productivity
  - Life satisfaction

- No stacking is used.

|---|---|---|

| Year | Temporal | Horizontal position as the two endpoints in each panel; year labels at top |
| Rank | Ordinal | Vertical position on y-axis; numeric rank labels |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual line identity across the two years |
| Highlight status (U.S. vs. other countries) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue and line weight (orange thick line for U.S., gray thin lines for others) |

raw_comment:
1. I notice that in 1990 the U.S. is #1, but by 2023 it only goes down by one to #2. However, I also notice that in the other two graphs the U.S. is lower. For example, in the “Productivity” graph, the U.S. starts down at #13, but goes up a little bit to #10. In the “Life Satisfaction” graph, the U.S. goes down from #5 to #10, showing that things have gotten worse in that department.

2. I wonder which countries are above the U.S., and why we haven’t taken more action to learn from them. I also wonder why the U.S. went down or up in certain graphs, and what led to it.

3. Countries in Control: Will The U.S. Keep Their Place at The Top?

raw_comment:
1. I notice that in the U.S the total G.D.P (Gross Domestic Product), it was ranked as the #1 country in 190, and still remained at the fairly high rank on #2. I also noticed how the amount of productivity went up within the past 18 years. I was surprised when I noticed how much life satisfaction went down. The life expectancy is extremely low, which isn’t something that I would expect. I also see how the trust in the federal government plummeted downwards in the past 17 years. I would’ve expected the U.S to be ranked much higher. I wonder why social isolation is decreasing so much. I also see how the average years of education remain the same.

2. I wonder if there is a way to tell if it is our country that is decreasing in the rank, or if it is just other countries increasing their rank.

3. This relates to my community and I because based on how the U.S is doing, our living conditions are different.

4. How much is the U.S actually doing for our country?

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that for the Trust in federal government graph, from 2006-2023, has decreased by a lot, since it was around in the middle in the beginning of the graph, while it ended near the bottom at the end of the graph. On the other hand, most of the governments have increased in this category. This puts the U.S as one of the lowest countries that have trust in the federal government. For the life expectancy graph, the U.S has dropped down 10 ranks, putting them near the bottom out of all other countries that are on the graph. 
2. I wonder why people are losing trust in the federal government in the U.S, and also why the life expectancy has been decreasing a lot. Why aren't the other countries experiencing a loss in their trust of the federal government, and how can we learn from that?
3.This can relate to me and my community since the federal government is considered one of the most important parts of the U.S, since they are needed to keep the country stable, and also the life expectancy can affect the people in my community and their future generations by changing how long they can actually live.
4. My title: "Connection through the Countries: Why is the U.S declining?"

raw_comment:
1.) I notice that, although things such as the G.D.P of America, as well as the average years of education one receives has changed infinitesimally for not at all, life expectancy, social isolation, and trust in the federal government, and even life satisfaction have decreased drastically, while productivity has risen. This could suggest that, although the country is overall very productive, the social structure of America, as well as the mental toll and health of its people, are in decline.

2.) Something I wondered about when looking at the graphs was, what is the main cause of the social decline of America’s people?

3.) This relates to me and my community because it is something that applies to so many people all across the globe, and isn’t just a fantasy. These unfortunate statistics are not just data, but experiences that so many people have had to go through, which could take a real toll on their mental and social health.

4.) A Culture in Decline: How the Land of the Free Fell From Grace

raw_comment:
I noticed that all the graphs are based on a general public observation. The total GDP in the first graph has decreased by one unit over the period of 33 years. Productivity has seemed to decrease, but on the graph it is represented in an increase of the line. The U.S. has been slower in producing their goods and services, and life satisfaction has noticeably decreased as the years progressed. In the second collection of graphs, the lines all share a similar pattern; they are decreasing in ranks compared to the other high income countries.

Why have many important and crucial pillars of our government decreased despite all of the “advancements” we seem to be having?

This relates to me and my community because despite the little changes we make within our town or state, the influence isn’t enough, and this is clear because we can see a decrease in rankings. Despite communities supposed to provide a supporting environment for people who live in it,  it is evident that humans are having more of a negative impact on communities themselves.

Title
Do our Opinions Really Have an Impact?

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed that the trust in the federal government has declined by 14. In 2006 the trust in the federal government was 20 from the years following that until 2023 the trust had declined. There are many drastic changes from other countries in their trust, but there are also countries that stay steady and have very similar numbers. 
I noticed that from the years 2015-2022 the average years of education has stayed the same, meaning that most people are getting the same amount of education in 2022 that they were in 2015.

What do you wonder?
I wonder what has caused countries to gain trust or lose trust, and why so drastically in some countries? Was the trust changed because of their person with power in that area or was if for other reasons

How does this relate to you and your community?
These graphs relate to our community because just like the graph shows people in the U.S are getting the same amount of education every year. This relates to me personally and my peers around me because we all hopefully are getting the same education for the same amount of time which is good.

Trust graph- Who are We Trusting and why, Take a Look Into Our Trust in the federal Government.

Education graph- How Long Were You in School,  Take a Look Into The Average years People are Taught.

## 1) Chart type
A set of **slope charts / rank-change line charts** showing country rankings between two years for several metrics.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: the visualization is split into multiple panels, one per metric:
  - Total G.D.P.
  - Productivity
  - Life satisfaction
  - Life expectancy
  - Trust in the federal government
  - Social isolation
  - Average years of education
- Within each panel, many country rank trajectories are shown as lines between two time points.
- **Highlighting**: the U.S. is emphasized with a thicker orange line; other countries are shown in thin gray lines.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Metric / indicator (Total G.D.P., Productivity, Life satisfaction, Life expectancy, Trust in the federal government, Social isolation, Average years of education) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Year | Temporal | Horizontal position as the two endpoints in each panel; year labels at top |
| Rank | Ordinal | Vertical position on y-axis; numeric rank labels |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual line identity across the two years |
| Highlight status (U.S. vs. other countries) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue and line weight (orange thick line for U.S., gray thin lines for others) |
| U.S. label / country annotation | Categorical/nominal | Text label (“U.S.” / “United States”) placed near highlighted line |
| Rank value annotations for highlighted country | Ordinal | Numeric text labels at line endpoints |

I wonder what is the main cause the ranks are going down over the years. 
This relates to me and my community because the economy of a country significantly  affects the people living in it.

raw_comment:
I notice that most graphs follow a downward trend except for productivity and education which remained the same. If I were to put the information into words, I would assume everything else is low because most of the U.S. is focusing on productivity and that enables less time for the things that also matter. 
I wonder why everything's going into a downward trend. How much factors are in play for this? The presidential election, Covid? Personally, I believe it's Covid because people were meant to isolate themselves from everybody and humans are social creatures. Isolation can get to someone. 
This relates to my community, especially the social isolation graph. It's difficult to communicate with people these days and understand them. Also, many students are obsessed with going to a good highschool for credibility they will use for future jobs. It's noted that people go through years of school to get a good job. It's evident in my school as well and doing that may lead to more productivity for the government, but more stress and less happy time. This is just a scenario, it's not relevant to all people, but based on the graphs, it probably is.
"The American Dream, Or Is It?: The Possible Downfall of the U.S.A's Workforce."

## 1) Chart type
A set of **slope charts / rank-change line charts** showing country rankings between two years for several metrics.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: the visualization is split into multiple panels, one per metric:
  - Total G.D.P.
  - Productivity
  - Life satisfaction
  - Life expectancy
  - Trust in the federal government
  - Social isolation
  - Average years of education
- Within each panel, many country rank trajectories are shown as lines between two time points.
- **Highlighting**: the U.S. is emphasized with a thicker orange line; other countries are shown in thin gray lines.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Metric / indicator (Total G.D.P., Productivity, Life satisfaction, Life expectancy, Trust in the federal government, Social isolation, Average years of education) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Year | Temporal | Horizontal position as the two endpoints in each panel; year labels at top |
| Rank | Ordinal | Vertical position on y-axis; numeric rank labels |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual line identity across the two years |
| Highlight status (U.S. vs. other countries) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue and line weight (orange thick line for U.S., gray thin lines for others) |
| U.S. label / country annotation | Categorical/nominal | Text label (“U.S.” / “United States”) placed near highlighted line |
| Rank value annotations for highlighted country | Ordinal | Numeric text labels at line endpoints |

raw_comment:
I analyzed the productivity graph as well as the life satisfaction graph.  

I noticed that over the years of 2005-2023 the U.S. ranking for productivity has increased, while the U.S. ranking for life satisfaction has decreased over the years. On the graph, the x axis represents the years throughout the graph, and the y axis represents the 38 different countries and their rank from 1-38. My headline for this graph is: What Really Makes Us satisfied?: productivity against life satisfaction.

## 1) Chart type
A set of **slope charts / rank-change line charts** showing country rankings between two years for several metrics.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: the visualization is split into multiple panels, one per metric:
  - Total G.D.P.
  - Productivity
  - Life satisfaction
  - Life expectancy
  - Trust in the federal government
  - Social isolation
  - Average years of education
- Within each panel, many country rank trajectories are shown as lines between two time points.
- **Highlighting**: the U.S. is emphasized with a thicker orange line; other countries are shown in thin gray lines.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Metric / indicator (Total G.D.P., Productivity, Life satisfaction, Life expectancy, Trust in the federal government, Social isolation, Average years of education) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Year | Temporal | Horizontal position as the two endpoints in each panel; year labels at top |
| Rank | Ordinal | Vertical position on y-axis; numeric rank labels |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual line identity across the two years |
| Highlight status (U.S. vs. other countries) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue and line weight (orange thick line for U.S., gray thin lines for others) |
| U.S. label / country annotation | Categorical/nominal | Text label (“U.S.” / “United States”) placed near highlighted line |

raw_comment:
Graphs: Productivity and Life Satisfaction

Notice: I notice than in the United States, when civilians are more productive and work more, that leads to less satisfaction. This graph reveals that these two aspects of life have an inverse causation relationship. 

Wonder: I wonder how the government is involved in this scenario. Was this relationship caused because of a specific presidential term or other government official? Could this data relate to inflation, low minimum wage, and controversy with salaries?

Relation to Community: This relates to my community because productivity applies to education as well. Many students often give back feedback to their schools, both positive and negative. The feedback may or may not be included into a school’s curriculum.

Headline: Money or Happiness?: What would you choose?

A set of **slope charts / rank-change line charts** showing country rankings between two years for several metrics.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: the visualization is split into multiple panels, one per metric:
  - Total G.D.P.
  - Productivity
  - Life satisfaction
  - Life expectancy
  - Trust in the federal government
  - Social isolation
  - Average years of education
- Within each panel, many country rank trajectories are shown as lines between two time points.
- **Highlighting**: the U.S. is emphasized with a thicker orange line; other countries are shown in thin gray lines.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Metric / indicator (Total G.D.P., Productivity, Life satisfaction, Life expectancy, Trust in the federal government, Social isolation, Average years of education) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Year | Temporal | Horizontal position as the two endpoints in each panel; year labels at top |
| Rank | Ordinal | Vertical position on y-axis; numeric rank labels |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual line identity across the two years |
| Highlight status (U.S. vs. other countries) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue and line weight (orange thick line for U.S., gray thin lines for others) |
| U.S. label / country annotation | Categorical/nominal | Text label (“U.S.” / “United States”) placed near highlighted line |
| Rank value annotations for highlighted country | Ordinal | Numeric text labels at line endpoints |

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that over the years, from 2005-2023, the United State’s ranking in productivity has increased from the 13th most productive country to the 10th most productive country. However, between the years 2006-2022, the life satisfaction ranking of the United States went down from the 5th to the 10th life satisfaction country. 
2. I wonder what caused the increase in productivity, and how that led to a decrease of life satisfaction. 
3. This relates to my community and I because we live in the U.S., and we should be aware of how our productivity, life satisfaction, and other factors have changed over the years. 
4. A headline could be, “How is America Really Doing? The Shocking Truth on What the People of the Land of Liberty are Thinking."

raw_comment:

This relates to my community as the nation and individual states all have separate leaders as years go on, so people may grow less satisfied as leaders change.

A set of **slope charts / rank-change line charts** showing country rankings between two years for several metrics.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: the visualization is split into multiple panels, one per metric:
  - Total G.D.P.
  - Productivity
  - Life satisfaction
  - Life expectancy
  - Trust in the federal government
  - Social isolation
  - Average years of education
- Within each panel, many country rank trajectories are shown as lines between two time points.
- **Highlighting**: the U.S. is emphasized with a thicker orange line; other countries are shown in thin gray lines.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Metric / indicator (Total G.D.P., Productivity, Life satisfaction, Life expectancy, Trust in the federal government, Social isolation, Average years of education) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Year | Temporal | Horizontal position as the two endpoints in each panel; year labels at top |
| Rank | Ordinal | Vertical position on y-axis; numeric rank labels |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual line identity across the two years |
| Highlight status (U.S. vs. other countries) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue and line weight (orange thick line for U.S., gray thin lines for others) |
| U.S. label / country annotation | Categorical/nominal | Text label (“U.S.” / “United States”) placed near highlighted line |
| Rank value annotations for highlighted country | Ordinal | Numeric text labels at line endpoints |

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that the U. S. decreased in ranking for Life Expectancy and Trust in Federal Government. I also notice that the top ranked country in Life Expectancy, continued to be the top 44 years later. The top five in Trust in the Federal Government, stayed consistently in the top 5.

What do you wonder?
I wonder how these graphs would look if it showed all of the years, rather than jumping from two years that are at least 18 years apart. Would there be a constant change in ranking for the U.S.? Or would it decrease and increase slowly?

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because we are part of the data that influences these graphs. We are part of the population that are experiencing the after effects of these rankings.

Create a catchy headline that captures the graphs’ main idea.
“The Truth: What are the American Citizens Experiencing?”

raw_comment:
1. For the Life Expectancy graph, in 1990-2023, the U.S had dropped ten ranks while most of the other countries have either increased or stayed in the same ranks. For the Trust in the Government graph, the U.S decreased by 14 ranks while most countries increased in their ranks.
2. I wonder, for both graphs, what is the main cause for the rapid decrease in the ranks? How has the U.S been dealing with these decreases? Are the same situations happening in other countries?
3. This relates to my community and I because even if we work really hard for changes, our actions can't influence the whole country. A lot of people are also losing trust in out government too.
4. A title for all of these graphs could be "Connecting Through Our Ranks: What Has Each Country Come To?"

raw_comment:
From 1990 to 2023, the U.S. life expectancy has dropped 10 ranks while the trust in the federal government from 2006 to 2023 has dropped by 14 ranks. Seeing the graph, I have started to wonder what the main cause of both graphs are to cause the ranks to be decreasing. I also wonder what other countries are experiencing something similar to this. How common is life expectancy and trust in the federal government dropping?  This relates to me and my community because we get a new "leader" for the U.S. every 4 years, lots of people often don't trust the new president. They are starting to lose trust in the federal government because of the leaders they chose to elect. People often don't trust the ideas of these new "leaders". The U.S. is also dropping in life expectancy because of the lack of effort people put into their everyday lives.

raw_comment:
I noticed that data about USA’s economy has shown that, overall, the country is doing well. However, USA’s ranking in categories related to their citizen’s personal lives (life satisfaction, life expectancy, and trust in federal government) has dropped 	significantly, most notably in trust in federal government, where America dropped 14 places from 2006 to 2023. 
I wonder why this stark contrast between America’s economy and personal wellbeing is happening, considering that it should have the means to improve its citizen’s lives. 
This relates to my community because the economy of a country directly affects the lives of the people living in it.

1.What do you notice?
The U.S. has had a declining life expectancy from 1990 to 2023. In 1990, the U.S. ranked at 19 for longest life expectancy and has declined to 29th place in 2023.
2.What do you wonder?
Throughout the many things that are happening in the world and in the U.S., what seems to be the largest thing that is killing the population?

Many things can happen which can cause deaths to people like faith, health, dangers, and many more.


Trust in Federal Government:
1.What do you notice?
From 2006 to 2023, the trust in the federal government for the U.S. has gradually declined. The country went from 20th place to 34th place, showing that the people of America over the years have less and less believed and trusted their own government.
2.What do you wonder?
What has caused this decline to start? What did the people see that made them realize that their government isn’t for them nor helping them?
3.How does this relate to you and your community?
Our community seems to also slowly give up on the government. In recent times, people in my own community have shown different signs towards the government. Some have given more trust, but have declined in the belief of a strong government, in any kind (local, county, state, national).

A good headline for these graphs would be: “The Plague of America”

A set of **slope charts / rank-change line charts** showing country rankings between two years for several metrics.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: the visualization is split into multiple panels, one per metric:
  - Total G.D.P.
  - Productivity
  - Life satisfaction
  - Life expectancy
  - Trust in the federal government
  - Social isolation
  - Average years of education
- Within each panel, many country rank trajectories are shown as lines between two time points.
- **Highlighting**: the U.S. is emphasized with a thicker orange line; other countries are shown in thin gray lines.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Metric / indicator (Total G.D.P., Productivity, Life satisfaction, Life expectancy, Trust in the federal government, Social isolation, Average years of education) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Year | Temporal | Horizontal position as the two endpoints in each panel; year labels at top |
| Rank | Ordinal | Vertical position on y-axis; numeric rank labels |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual line identity across the two years |
| Highlight status (U.S. vs. other countries) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue and line weight (orange thick line for U.S., gray thin lines for others) |
| U.S. label / country annotation | Categorical/nominal | Text label (“U.S.” / “United States”) placed near highlighted line |
| Rank value annotations for highlighted country | Ordinal | Numeric text labels at line endpoints |

raw_comment: While the productivity of America has increased, life satisfaction of the average person has gone down over the years. The increase in productivity shows that each person is on average working more or at least working harder to become more productive. However, the decrease in life satisfaction shows that with the increased amount of work, people are less happy and satisfied compared to the past. Moreover, as society has hit a social low in the pandemic, more people are starting to prioritize work over joy like socializing. Additionally, people have also been impacted financially, meaning people also need to work more to make ends meet. These two graphs being opposite of each other shows the working class becoming more productive to keep their quality of life like having a stable job, even when it is actually decreasing their overall life satisfaction.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed that social isolation drastically decreased in the U.S. However, it only really decreased in our country and a few others. Social isolation increased in ranks for many other countries. The countries that have decreased in social isolation probably just have less social isolation than other countries, even if they have a lot.

What do you wonder?
Does the increase in cyberbullying contribute to an increase in social isolation in other countries? Did the United States get a lower ranking because of their approach to end cyberbullying at schools?

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because in our school, cyberbullying and bullying is taken very seriously, and because our school talks about including others, social isolation in our community decreases over time.

raw_comment:
1. I notice that even though we have become more productive in the past few years, people are much less satisfied with their lives. While we have increased three positions in productivity, we have dropped by five positions in the life satisfaction category. 

2. I wonder if there is any connection between productivity and life satisfaction, as while many always say that being active and productive makes you happy, this graph points towards the opposite of the previously mentioned statement, showing that productivity could connect to less life satisfaction. 

3. People who surround me, and those in my community, all work hard to be a part of this community. They work together to build a nicer town and area for everyone. Yet, this graph points out that while many of us are being productive, maybe we still do not feel satisfied, trying to reach a goal that we may never hit, which makes life satisfaction lower. 

4. Connections Going Unnoticed; How Could These Different Aspects of American Life Connect?

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
A set of **slope charts / rank-change line charts** showing country rankings between two years for several metrics.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: the visualization is split into multiple panels, one per metric:
  - Total G.D.P.
  - Productivity
  - Life satisfaction
  - Life expectancy
  - Trust in the federal government
  - Social isolation
  - Average years of education
- Within each panel, many country rank trajectories are shown as lines between two time points.
- **Highlighting**: the U.S. is emphasized with a thicker orange line; other countries are shown in thin gray lines.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Metric / indicator (Total G.D.P., Productivity, Life satisfaction, Life expectancy, Trust in the federal government, Social isolation, Average years of education) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Year | Temporal | Horizontal position as the two endpoints in each panel; year labels at top |
| Rank | Ordinal | Vertical position on y-axis; numeric rank labels |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual line identity across the two years |
| Highlight status (U.S. vs. other countries) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue and line weight (orange thick line for U.S., gray thin lines for others) |
| U.S. label / country annotation | Categorical/nominal | Text label (“U.S.” / “United States”) placed near highlighted line |
| Rank value annotations for highlighted country | Ordinal | Numeric text labels at line endpoints |
raw_comment:
1. I notice that an overall trend in all the graphs is that the U.S ranking has gone down. Some anomalies present are the graph about the total years of education, because the ranking stayed the same. Additionally the graph about Productivity shows that the U.S has improved over the years. I have also noticed that our ranking has gone down most in our trust for the government. This can be because more Americans don’t agree with our government's system, and also because they don’t agree with the new leaders in place, as all presidents are controversial.
2. I wonder what has improved our productivity. Additionally, as our debt continues to grow, how is the productivity department helping reduce that?
3. These graphs relate to my community as I am able to notice different trends. Most people in my community have gone to college for the same number of years contributing to the school year average. Also, the Life Satisfaction graph, as you are able to ask people what they expected to be and what they are now. 
4. Is Life in the U.S Really that Much Better

Wonder: I wonder if this is correlation or causation. Does the increase in productivity in the U.S. over an 18 year period directly cause a shorter life expectancy (perhaps due to overworking), or is this simply coincidence?
Relevance: This relates to my community because it is harder to see decreases in life expectancy at such small scales. At a national level, data shows a steady decline, seemingly due to more intense professional demands, yet it still impacts individuals even if not immediately apparent.
Potential Headline: “The Inadvertent Detriment that Increased Productivity is on the U.S.A”

A set of **slope charts / rank-change line charts** showing country rankings between two years for several metrics.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: the visualization is split into multiple panels, one per metric:
  - Total G.D.P.
  - Productivity
  - Life satisfaction
  - Life expectancy
  - Trust in the federal government
  - Social isolation
  - Average years of education
- Within each panel, many country rank trajectories are shown as lines between two time points.
- **Highlighting**: the U.S. is emphasized with a thicker orange line; other countries are shown in thin gray lines.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Metric / indicator (Total G.D.P., Productivity, Life satisfaction, Life expectancy, Trust in the federal government, Social isolation, Average years of education) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Year | Temporal | Horizontal position as the two endpoints in each panel; year labels at top |
| Rank | Ordinal | Vertical position on y-axis; numeric rank labels |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual line identity across the two years |
| Highlight status (U.S. vs. other countries) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue and line weight (orange thick line for U.S., gray thin lines for others) |
| U.S. label / country annotation | Categorical/nominal | Text label (“U.S.” / “United States”) placed near highlighted line |
| Rank value annotations for highlighted country | Ordinal | Numeric text labels at line endpoints |

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
A set of **slope charts / rank-change line charts** showing country rankings between two years for several metrics.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: the visualization is split into multiple panels, one per metric:
  - Total G.D.P.
  - Productivity
  - Life satisfaction
  - Life expectancy
  - Trust in the federal government
  - Social isolation
  - Average years of education
- Within each panel, many country rank trajectories are shown as lines between two time points.
- **Highlighting**: the U.S. is emphasized with a thicker orange line; other countries are shown in thin gray lines.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Metric / indicator (Total G.D.P., Productivity, Life satisfaction, Life expectancy, Trust in the federal government, Social isolation, Average years of education) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Year | Temporal | Horizontal position as the two endpoints in each panel; year labels at top |
| Rank | Ordinal | Vertical position on y-axis; numeric rank labels |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual line identity across the two years |
| Highlight status (U.S. vs. other countries) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue and line weight (orange thick line for U.S., gray thin lines for others) |
| U.S. label / country annotation | Categorical/nominal | Text label (“U.S.” / “United States”) placed near highlighted line |
| Rank value annotations for highlighted country | Ordinal | Numeric text labels at line endpoints |

raw_comment:
From 1990 to 2023, the U.S’ life expectancy has dropped 10 rankings. Seeing the graph, also, I have come to wonder which countries have experienced the most significant rises in ranking regarding life expectancy and satisfaction. Also, this graph relates to me, as an American citizen, as it is suggesting that the U.S, once having been a ‘leader’ in multiple sectors, is ‘falling from grace’, being beaten by former countries that the U.S had formerly excelled against. Seeing such information, it can be suggested that the U.S' development is now somewhat lacking[at least compared to other countries' development considering the U.S' prior triumph in such]. A title I came up with was:
The American Decline: The U.S’ Fall From Its Status as a 'Superpower'.

A set of **slope charts / rank-change line charts** showing country rankings between two years for several metrics.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: the visualization is split into multiple panels, one per metric:
  - Total G.D.P.
  - Productivity
  - Life satisfaction
  - Life expectancy
  - Trust in the federal government
  - Social isolation
  - Average years of education
- Within each panel, many country rank trajectories are shown as lines between two time points.
- **Highlighting**: the U.S. is emphasized with a thicker orange line; other countries are shown in thin gray lines.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Metric / indicator (Total G.D.P., Productivity, Life satisfaction, Life expectancy, Trust in the federal government, Social isolation, Average years of education) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Year | Temporal | Horizontal position as the two endpoints in each panel; year labels at top |
| Rank | Ordinal | Vertical position on y-axis; numeric rank labels |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual line identity across the two years |
| Highlight status (U.S. vs. other countries) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue and line weight (orange thick line for U.S., gray thin lines for others) |

3) These graphs are made up of my country, which includes my community. My community impacts this graph, but not on a large scale, due to the fact that the U.S is so big.

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
A set of **slope charts / rank-change line charts** showing country rankings between two years for several metrics.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: the visualization is split into multiple panels, one per metric:
  - Total G.D.P.
  - Productivity
  - Life satisfaction
  - Life expectancy
  - Trust in the federal government
  - Social isolation
  - Average years of education
- Within each panel, many country rank trajectories are shown as lines between two time points.
- **Highlighting**: the U.S. is emphasized with a thicker orange line; other countries are shown in thin gray lines.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Metric / indicator (Total G.D.P., Productivity, Life satisfaction, Life expectancy, Trust in the federal government, Social isolation, Average years of education) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Year | Temporal | Horizontal position as the two endpoints in each panel; year labels at top |
| Rank | Ordinal | Vertical position on y-axis; numeric rank labels |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual line identity across the two years |
| Highlight status (U.S. vs. other countries) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue and line weight (orange thick line for U.S., gray thin lines for others) |
| U.S. label / country annotation | Categorical/nominal | Text label (“U.S.” / “United States”) placed near highlighted line |
| Rank value annotations for highlighted country | Ordinal | Numeric text labels at line endpoints |
raw_comment:
Looking at the graphs in these articles, they compare the rankings of certain years. If we look at the graph called "Productivity" we can see our productivity increased from 2005 to 2023. However, if we look below that the life satisfactory has decreased from 2006 to 2022. Both of these graphs covered a similar amount of time which could possibly mean they are correlated. Despite the fact that our productivity has increased, the graph shows that people have become less satisfied with their life and the progress they have made. 

If we scroll down and look at the bottom four graphs. Three graphs show a large decrease while one graph is flat lined. In the three graphs with a negative linear relationship,  we notice that people have lost there trust in the federal government, have become more socially isolated, and don't expect much from life. Why are many of these graphs declining. This is a story the New York Times should investigate.
